standard.title: Pythagoras' Theorem
standard.description: use Pythagoras' theorem to solve problems involving the side lengths of right-angled triangles
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify perfect squares, square roots, and right-angled triangles (from AC9M7N01, AC9M7SP02). Students have informal exposure to the 3-4-5 triangle.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students state and apply Pythagoras' theorem to find unknown side lengths in right-angled triangles in practical and geometric contexts.

nodes.label: Understanding and stating Pythagoras' theorem
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students state Pythagoras' theorem (a² + b² = c²) and understand it as a relationship between areas of squares on the sides of a right-angled triangle.
nodes.minimum_width: State the theorem and identify which side is the hypotenuse; verify the theorem holds for a 3-4-5 triangle.
nodes.typical_width: Verify the theorem using area diagrams or proofs from multiple cultural traditions; state the converse; identify Pythagorean triples.
wider: Investigate different applications, demonstrations and proofs of Pythagoras' theorem from multiple cultures: Egypt, Mesopotamia, India, China, and Greece — compare the approaches.
Identify Pythagorean triples systematically: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (7,24,25), (8,15,17) — investigate how to generate new triples from known ones.

response_modes.reason: Proofs from multiple cultural traditions enrich understanding of the theorem and demonstrate it is not exclusively a Western mathematical result. Multiple verification methods also build confidence before applying the theorem.

nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 application requires students to identify the hypotenuse and set up a² + b² = c² correctly — students who have only memorised a formula without understanding the area relationship misidentify the hypotenuse or set up the equation incorrectly, producing systematically wrong answers.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Multi-cultural proof histories and systematic generation of Pythagorean triples offer advancing students rich mathematical and historical depth — the theorem's appearance across multiple ancient civilisations is a genuinely fascinating conceptual extension.
success_criteria: States Pythagoras' theorem correctly and identifies the hypotenuse.
Verifies the theorem for at least one specific case.
States the converse: if a² + b² = c² then the triangle is right-angled.

nodes.label: Finding unknown side lengths using Pythagoras
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students apply Pythagoras' theorem to find the hypotenuse or a shorter side in right-angled triangles, including in practical and coordinate geometry contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Find the hypotenuse and find a shorter side given the other two sides for at least two examples.
nodes.typical_width: Apply the theorem to varied practical problems; identify right-angled triangles within diagrams; apply to distance between two points on the Cartesian plane.
wider: Apply the theorem to 3D problems: find the diagonal of a rectangular prism using the theorem twice.
Investigate how Pythagoras' theorem can determine distance between two points on a Cartesian plane — connect to applications in predictive text and mapping.

response_modes.reason: Applying Pythagoras requires first identifying the right-angled triangle within a diagram. Students who only practise decontextualised calculations fail to identify the relevant triangle in applied problems.

nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 triangle classification requires comparing a² + b² with c² — students who cannot fluently apply the theorem to find unknown sides (and who misidentify c as the longest side) apply the classification test to the wrong quantities.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: 3D applications and the distance formula connection offer advancing students genuinely rich extensions — applying the theorem twice to find a 3D diagonal is a satisfying and accessible multi-step challenge within Year 8.
success_criteria: Correctly identifies the hypotenuse in a given right-angled triangle.
Finds an unknown side correctly using the theorem.
Applies the theorem to a practical problem context.

nodes.label: Classifying triangles using side lengths
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students use the relationship between a² + b² and c² to classify triangles as right-angled, acute or obtuse.
nodes.minimum_width: Given three side lengths, determine whether the triangle is right-angled, acute or obtuse.
nodes.typical_width: Apply the classification rule across a range of triangles; explain the reasoning for acute (a² + b² > c²) and obtuse (a² + b² < c²) cases.
wider: Investigate why the inequality changes direction for acute and obtuse triangles — connect to the geometric argument about how the angle affects the opposite side length.
Apply classification to survey and construction contexts: verify whether a corner is square using the converse of Pythagoras.

response_modes.reason: Triangle classification requires comparing a² + b² with c² and reasoning about the direction of the inequality. Students need an explicit reasoning scaffold to apply this reliably.

success_criteria: Correctly classifies a triangle given three side lengths.
States the rule for each classification (right, acute, obtuse).
Identifies the longest side as c before applying the test.
